Paper Title: Co-Creating Accessibility-Centred Mobility Strategies in Low-Density Suburban Contexts: Evidence from Coimbra, Portugal
Study type / basis for inclusion: Primary fieldwork. Three deliberative focus groups the authors ran themselves; a case where the design process deliberately equalised institutional and citizen input.
Case setting: Sao Martinho do Bispo, a low-density suburban parish on Coimbra's southwestern periphery, Portugal (about 13,000 residents, 21 square km, ageing traditional cores plus newer housing, steep topography, one operator SMTUC with roughly one hundred stops). Run inside the ENTROPY project. Citizen participants were predominantly older adults, average ages above 60 (p. 7).
Method(s), session by session: Three focus groups in Sao Martinho do Bispo, March to April 2025, 18 participants (institutional, technical, citizen), recruited via local associations, municipal contacts, and institutional partnerships. Institutional/technical and citizen participants met in separate groups to reduce power asymmetries (p. 7). Each session about 90 minutes, four phases: (1) trust building (not analysed), (2) open debate on six predefined strategies plus a green/yellow/red visual vote, (3) individual proposals worked up collaboratively on detailed maps of the study area, then colour-coded assessment, (4) an autonomous individual prioritisation via digital scoring (Slido, 1 to 5 Likert) of a separate proposal set introduced by the research team (p. 5 to 6). Sessions recorded and transcribed, then coded in Atlas.ti 25 with a hybrid inductive-deductive scheme, single coder, co-occurrence coefficient threshold c at least 0.20 (p. 8). A final co-creation phase consolidated eight strategies, each cross-checked against the co-occurrence results (p. 21 to 22).
Tools and artifacts: Six predefined strategy prompts as a shared reference; green/yellow/red visual voting cards; detailed printed maps of the study area for spatial diagnosis; Slido online polling with a five-point Likert scale; Atlas.ti 25 for coding and co-occurrence analysis; session recordings and transcripts triangulated with field observation and documentary sources (p. 4). The 15-Minute City, Transit-Oriented Development, and Mobility as a Service were carried in as analytical lenses, not templates (p. 2).
Underlying principle of the method: Grounded in collaborative and communicative planning (Healey; Innes and Booher; Forester), aiming to bridge expert and experiential knowledge (p. 4, p. 16). Group separation to mitigate power asymmetries and foster open deliberation (p. 7). In the synthesis phase, outputs from all groups were treated as analytically equivalent with no hierarchical weighting between institutional, technical, or citizen inputs (p. 24). Mobility framed as a social right rather than solely a matter of efficiency (p. 2).
Provocation used to generate new ideas: Yes. Six predefined strategies were used as a shared conceptual framework to stimulate reflection and identify structural barriers and opportunities (p. 5). Detailed maps prompted participants to locate spatial inequalities and formulate territorial proposals (p. 5). Global proximity models (15-Minute City, TOD, MaaS) were reframed as things to reinterpret rather than adopt (p. 2, p. 23). The phase-four proposal set was introduced by the research team specifically to test preferences (p. 15).
Who holds design authority: Shared but framed by the research team (ENTROPY project, TRANSyT at UPM Madrid, University of Extremadura, University of Coimbra), which set the predefined strategies and proposal set and did all coding (single coder, p. 8). Institutional, technical, and citizen stakeholders co-created the eight strategies; the synthesis applied no hierarchical weighting (p. 24). Implementation authority is split: infrastructure strategies depend on municipal authorities and transport operators, awareness and behavioural strategies on schools, local associations, and community organisations (p. 23 to 24). Object is the mobility service, network, and street redesign, not statutory policy.
What is being designed: Eight co-created sustainable mobility strategies for Sao Martinho do Bispo: pedestrian infrastructure and public-space redesign; cycling infrastructure and services; regulation of private transport and parking; education, awareness, and a culture of sustainable mobility; public transport frequency, reliability, and real-time information; mobility plans for schools and workplaces; road-space reallocation toward pedestrians and cyclists with an equity and safety focus; integrated spatial planning (Table 5, p. 22). Framed as an initial deliberative step; the study does not evaluate long-term implementation feasibility (p. 24).
Values surfaced in the case: Institutional and technical actors emphasised efficiency, coordination, system rationality, and long-term planning, and were cautious about new investment citing efficiency and maintenance (p. 6, p. 13, p. 16). Citizens emphasised everyday accessibility, walkability, reliability, comfort, and safety, with usability and reliability taking precedence over systemic innovation (p. 15, p. 16). Shared across groups: accessibility, connectivity, safe continuous pedestrian networks. Relational trust recurs: acceptance of restrictive measures and of multimodal projects was said to rely on trust, fairness, and transparent communication more than technical design (p. 14, p. 19). Flexibility for variable need appears as a warning that digital-only systems risk excluding older and digitally vulnerable users, requiring analogue alternatives (p. 18, p. 23).
Ideal traveler per decision-makers: Not named as an ideal traveler construct. Institutional and technical actors' priorities imply a traveler served by diversified modal options and integrated digital services: their top scores went to cycling infrastructure, shared mobility, and pedestrian zones, reflecting an understanding of mobility as dependent on multimodality and digitalisation and a shift toward integrated mobility ecosystems and MaaS (p. 15). A municipal representative benchmarked transit against the private car: 'It is inconceivable that a public transport route takes 50 min when the same trip by car takes 15' (p. 13). A health-sector participant framed the rational traveler as one who weighs cost and time: 'Many young people call an Uber, not realising that if they wait five minutes, they spend 10 times less and take 15 min longer' (p. 18).
Actual travelers encountered: Citizen participants were mostly older adults, retired residents and active workers relying on walking, public transport, and private vehicles, in an area whose steep slopes constrain active travel for older residents and people with reduced mobility (p. 7, p. 9). Their stated needs: continuous pavements (currently 'forced to walk along drainage ditches', p. 13), reliable and frequent buses, real-time information, safe crossings. Cautious interest in shared mobility, influenced by limited familiarity with these emerging systems (p. 15). People with disabilities, migrants, and younger low-income residents were largely absent from the room (p. 24 to 25).
Gap between the two: Institutional actors emphasised efficiency, coordination, long-term planning, and technological or MaaS solutions and were wary of new spending; citizens wanted concrete daily improvements, walkability, and reliability, and were wary of digital-only systems. On new facilities the split was sharp: institutional and technical participants (n equals 13) voted mostly red (8 negative), citizens (n equals 5) mostly green (3 positive) (p. 13). The paper reads this as complementarity between institutional rationality and citizen pragmatism rather than open conflict, and credits the deliberative design and no-weighting synthesis with partly reconciling it (p. 15, p. 24).
Quotable moment: "The divergence reflects differing priorities: institutional actors emphasised efficiency and maintenance, whereas citizens focused on everyday accessibility." (p. 13). On the process itself: "outputs from all groups were treated as analytically equivalent and systematically compared, with no hierarchical weighting between institutional, technical, or citizen inputs" (p. 24).
Cross-comparison note (our synthesis): A rare documented case where the process design itself refused to let technical actors set the terms: the no-hierarchical-weighting synthesis (p. 24) is close to a working model of the participation our paper argues AV deployment skips. The institutional-versus-citizen split it surfaces (efficiency, coordination, and system rationality on one side; walkability, reliability, and everyday access on the other) maps directly onto our efficiency-versus-community-values axis, and here it was visible in the room rather than only in outcomes. Useful as a counter-model. Caveats: the citizen sample skewed to older adults with no people with disabilities or younger low-income residents, so flexibility for variable need is only partly represented; this is strategy co-creation, not vehicle or service design, and it stops before implementation.

Paper Title: Transportation barriers and equity: Values and experiences of elected officials
Study type / basis for inclusion: Primary fieldwork and a decision-maker paper. A national survey plus 38 interviews the authors ran with elected officials; supplies the decision-maker side of the ideal-traveler contrast with direct evidence.
Case setting: Canadian municipal and regional elected officials (mayors and councilors) in jurisdictions that have some form of public transit. 165 survey respondents across seven provinces and one territory; 38 follow-up interviewees. Sample skews senior (41 percent) and to smaller communities; under 10 percent identify as racialized, disabled, Indigenous, LGBTQ+, or immigrant (p. 7 to 8).
Method(s), session by session: Mixed method. (1) National online survey, open June to September 2022 (note 3), sent to 2,148 mayors and councilors via a university survey centre with two follow-up emails, 165 completed responses, 8.2 percent response rate, about 25 minutes each. Three themes: personal experience with transportation barriers; sources of knowledge; equity values via forced-choice paired statements; plus demographics and travel behaviour. Instrument developed in consultation with the Mobilizing Justice research partnership (academics, practitioners, community advocates) and grounded in Linovski et al. 2021 (p. 6 to 7). (2) 38 key-informant interviews, January to March 2023, 20 minutes to 1 hour, with survey respondents who opted in; transcribed and coded in Dedoose using the framework method, codes tested on a sample and reviewed by multiple team members (p. 6). (3) Preliminary findings presented to the Community and Equity Advisory Table affiliated with Mobilizing Justice (note 15).
Tools and artifacts: Six forced-choice value pairs (Table 7): procedural fairness, mode-choice fairness, geographic fairness, utilitarian versus targeted, maintenance of existing conditions, willingness to pay; respondent picks one of two statements. A barrier ranking exercise for self and for constituents (Table 5). A deliberately unprimed interview question, 'What populations or groups of people do you think of when considering transportation barriers?', with no option list (p. 12). Census-aligned mode-of-travel questions. Dedoose qualitative software.
Underlying principle of the method: Policy-learning theory: decision-making as a mix of personal experience, network exposure, and evidence (p. 4 to 5). The study deliberately treats elected officials as endogenous to transportation decision-making, against a technical-rational tradition that treats politicians as exogenous to the process (Marsden and Reardon, cited p. 2). Centering the decision-maker's own values and lived experience as the object of study, on the premise that who decides shapes distribution. Uses the category approach to equity groups while noting its limits (Church et al., cited p. 3).
Provocation used to generate new ideas: Limited and not a design provocation. The forced-choice value pairs act as elicitation devices, each forcing a choice between a mainstream-equity statement and a competing utilitarian, geographic, or status-quo statement to surface latent values (p. 13 to 14). The unprimed interview question was designed so respondents would develop their own responses rather than be primed with a list of options (p. 12). No prototypes, scenarios, or ideation exercises; the instrument provokes articulation of existing values, not generation of new mobility ideas.
Who holds design authority: The research team (planning academics at the University of Manitoba and University of Waterloo, and United Way Greater Toronto), with the survey instrument co-developed with the Mobilizing Justice partnership and reviewed by named advisors. The study's subjects, elected officials, hold real decision authority over long-range planning, infrastructure, services, and resource allocation (p. 6), but as participants they design nothing here. Scope: this is about who sets transportation investment priorities; it does not itself design a service, vehicle, or network.
What is being designed: Nothing designed. Diagnostic study of decision-makers' values. Its practical recommendation is that planning staff and advocates engage elected officials in policy learning early, before officials are charged with making decisions (p. 17).
Values surfaced in the case: Utilitarian greatest-good dominates: 63 percent chose transportation policies that 'provide benefits to the greatest number of people' over prioritising marginalised people and communities (37 percent) (Table 7, Q4). Procedural fairness endorsed in the abstract: 73 percent agreed consultation is only fair if people from different identities and communities can fully participate (Q1, p. 13). 84 percent accept that existing costs or infrastructure sometimes need to change for fairness (Q5); 77 percent say car users should pay the full costs of driving (Q6). Geographic fairness near evenly split, 56 percent prioritise historically underinvested areas versus 44 percent equal investment everywhere (Q3). Mode-choice equity endorsed in principle by 66 percent (Q2). Support for equity-targeted values rises with personal or close-relation experience of barriers, with being a woman (60 percent of those prioritising marginalised groups), and with larger community size (p. 14 to 15). Officials rely most on staff reports (81 percent regularly) and least on advocacy groups (40 percent) and constituent associations (47 percent) (p. 12 to 13).
Ideal traveler per decision-makers: The paper does not use the term. Its value data imply a traveler who is a member of the general public counted in 'the greatest number' (63 percent, Q4), for whom transportation investment is a community-wide good rather than targeted redress, and who most likely owns a car: 90 percent of officials have at least one household car and 71 percent drive to work, no respondent used paratransit or ride-hailing for any trip (p. 8). Officials reported little direct experience of the barriers under discussion: 5 percent a mobility-limiting disability, 6 percent inability to afford transit, 7 percent harassment (p. 9). A councilor named the mental model directly (p. 12, quoted below).
Actual travelers encountered: Surfaced second-hand through officials' interview accounts, not collected from travelers. Examples officials gave: a 96-year-old living with her son in a mobile home, out of food, with no transportation (Interview 38, p. 12); a growing newcomer and refugee population who do not feel comfortable 'due to the racism or the sexism, and exhibited violence on transit' (Interview 23, p. 12); residents pushed 'further and further from the core' into cheap suburban housing with infrequent transit (Interview 26, p. 12). Officials most often named people with disabilities (66 percent), low income (58 percent), and seniors (45 percent) as facing barriers; immigrants, women, and racialized people were rarely named (Table 6, p. 11 to 12).
Gap between the two: 73 percent endorse fully inclusive consultation but only 37 percent would prioritise marginalised communities in investment (p. 13 to 14). The paper names this 'a significant disconnect between academic and professional understandings of equity and the values of many elected officials' (p. 16) and opens with the nested quote 'a fundamental mismatch between who is making key transit decisions . . . and who is most affected by those decisions' (p. 2, quoting TransitCenter, 2022, p. 5). Officials' thin direct experience of affordability, disability, and harassment barriers tracks with their lower support for equity-targeted values (p. 16).
Quotable moment: ". . . those people are in the habit of thinking, you know, that everybody has a house and a car. Well, not everybody has both, and not everybody has either." (p. 12, councilor, Interview 19).
Cross-comparison note (our synthesis): This paper supplies the decision-maker side of our contrast with direct evidence rather than inference: a majority of Canadian local elected officials hold a utilitarian, community-wide-benefit view of transportation investment (63 percent), own cars (90 percent), and have little first-hand experience of the barriers under discussion, while endorsing inclusive process in the abstract (73 percent). That profile is the implicit ideal traveler our fieldwork participants are measured against. The paper's own framing, an academic and professional versus political values gap, parallels our engineering-efficiency versus community-values axis and shows the mismatch sits upstream of any particular technology, already present in who sets priorities. Caveats: 8.2 percent response rate with self-selection toward officials with strong transportation views; the traveler evidence here is second-hand through officials' accounts.
